Deflection is proportional to current, so a reduction from 30 to 20 divisions means the
current must fall to **two thirds**.
**Step 1 — find the original current.**
I₁ = V/(G + R)
= 3/(50 + 2950)
= 3/3000
= **1 x 10⁻³ A** ✓ giving 30 divisions.
**Step 2 — find the current needed for 20 divisions.** Deflection ∝ current:
I₂ = (20/30) x 10⁻³
= **(2/3) x 10⁻³ A**
**Step 3 — find the total resistance that gives that current.**
R_total = V/I₂
= 3/(2/3 x 10⁻³)
= 4·5 x 10³
= **4500 Ω**
**Step 4 — find the extra resistance.** The circuit already has 3000 Ω:
R_extra = 4500 − 3000
= **1500 Ω** ✓
**Why the extra resistance is only half of the original.** To cut the current to two
thirds, the total resistance must rise to **three halves** of its value ✓ 3000 x 1·5 =
4500, so only 1500 Ω more is needed - not another 3000 Ω.
**A check on the new deflection.**
I = 3/4500 = **0·667 mA**
and 0·667/1·0 x 30 = **20 divisions** ✓ exactly as required.
**The general relation.** For deflections θ₁ and θ₂ with the same source,
R₂/R₁ = θ₁/θ₂ ✓
Here 4500/3000 = 30/20 = 1·5 ✓ a one-line route to the answer.
**Why "additional" matters.** The question asks for the resistance to be **added**, not
the new total ✓ Answering 4500 Ω would be answering a different question - and the
40 Ω difference between 2950 and 3000 shows that the galvanometer's own resistance must
be kept in the total throughout.
**Reading the distractors.** **2950 Ω** ✗ would double the resistance and cut the
deflection to 15 divisions. **4440 Ω** and **7400 Ω** ✗ overshoot further, giving about
11 and 8 divisions ✓ Substituting each candidate and recomputing the deflection tests
them directly.
∴ 1500 Ω.

Compare the field at the centre with the field on the axis; the ratio depends only on
x/R.
**Step 1 — write the two fields.**
at the centre: B_c = μ₀I/(2R)
on the axis at distance x: B_a = μ₀IR²/[2(R² + x²)^(3/2)] ✓
**Step 2 — form the ratio.**
B_c/B_a = [μ₀I/(2R)] x [2(R² + x²)^(3/2)/(μ₀IR²)]
= **(R² + x²)^(3/2)/R³**
**Step 3 — set it equal to 5√5.** Note that 5√5 = **5^(3/2)**:
(R² + x²)^(3/2)/R³ = 5^(3/2)
**Step 4 — raise both sides to the power 2/3.**
(R² + x²)/R² = 5
R² + x² = 5R²
x² = 4R²
**x = 2R** ✓
**Step 5 — substitute R = 0·1 m.**
x = 2(0·1) = **0·2 m** ✓
**Why 5√5 is the clue.** Writing it as 5^(3/2) matches the 3/2 power in the field
formula exactly ✓ Recognising that turns an awkward-looking equation into a simple one -
and the examiner chose the number for precisely that reason.
**A check by direct substitution.** With R = 0·1 and x = 0·2:
(R² + x²)^(3/2) = (0·01 + 0·04)^(3/2) = (0·05)^(3/2) = **0·01118**
R³ = **0·001**
ratio = 11·18, and 5√5 = **11·18** ✓ exact.
**How the axial field behaves.** It falls off steadily from μ₀I/2R at the centre, and far
away, where x ≫ R, it goes as **1/x³** - the familiar dipole fall-off ✓ At x = 2R the
field has already dropped to about a ninth of its central value.
**Reading the distractors.** **0·1 m** ✗ is x = R, which gives a ratio of 2^(3/2) =
2·83. **0·05 m** ✗ gives 1·40, and **0·25 m** ✗ gives 18·2 ✓ Only x = 2R produces
11·18, and substituting each candidate checks it in one step.
∴ 0.2 m.

"Suspended in mid-air" means the magnetic force exactly **balances the weight**.
**Step 1 — write the magnetic force.** The current is horizontal and the field is into
the page, so the two are perpendicular:
F = BIL
= (0·5)(2·5)(0·5)
= **0·625 N** ✓ and by F̄ = I L̄ x B̄ it points **upward**, which is what holds the wire
up.
**Step 2 — set it equal to the weight.**
BIL = mg
0·625 = m(10)
**Step 3 — solve.**
m = 0·625/10
= 0·0625 kg
= **62·5 g** ✓
**Why the length must be in metres.** 50 cm = **0·5 m** ✓ Leaving it as 50 would make
the force a hundred times too large and the mass 6·25 kg.
**Checking the direction of the force.** With the current to the **right** and B
**into** the page, I L̄ x B̄ points **upward** ✓ If the field were out of the page the
force would be downward and the wire could not be supported at all - the geometry
matters as much as the magnitude.
**How strong this arrangement is.** A current of 2·5 A in a 0·5 T field supports only
62·5 g over half a metre ✓ Magnetic levitation of anything substantial needs either very
large currents or superconducting magnets, which is why maglev trains use both.
**A check by rearranging.** If the mass really were 62·5 g:
mg = 0·0625 x 10 = **0·625 N**
BIL = 0·5 x 2·5 x 0·5 = **0·625 N** ✓ balanced.
**Reading the distractors.** **125 g** ✗ weighs 1·25 N, twice the available magnetic
force - the wire would fall. **250 g** ✗ and **100 g** ✗ are heavier still ✓ Any mass
above 62·5 g simply cannot be held by this force.
∴ 62.5 gm.

Note: the printed key gives the third option, 125 gm. Equating BIL = mg with B = 0·5 T,
I = 2·5 A and L = 0·5 m gives a force of 0·625 N and hence m = 0·0625 kg = 62·5 g; a
125 g wire would weigh twice the force available. The key has been corrected to the
first option.

The **saturation current** measures the intensity, and the graph shows I₂ saturating
higher.
**Step 1 — read the two curves.** Both rise and then flatten off, but the curve labelled
I₂ levels out at a **higher** photocurrent than the one labelled I₁ ✓
**Step 2 — interpret the saturation level.** At saturation, **every** photoelectron
emitted is collected ✓ so the saturation current is proportional to the **number** of
electrons released per second, which in turn is proportional to the number of photons
arriving - that is, to the **intensity**.
**Step 3 — conclude.**
**I₁ < I₂** ✓ the second beam is the more intense.
**Step 4 — note what the graph shows is the same.** Both curves meet the voltage axis at
the **same** stopping potential −V₀ ✓ The stopping potential depends only on the
**frequency** of the light, not on its intensity, so the two beams have the same colour
and differ only in brightness.
**The two independent facts of photoelectricity.**
**intensity** fixes the **number** of electrons, hence the saturation current ✓
**frequency** fixes the **maximum kinetic energy**, hence the stopping potential ✓
Einstein's equation, eV₀ = hν − φ, contains no intensity term at all - which is exactly
why classical wave theory failed to explain the effect.
**What a change of frequency would look like.** The curves would meet the axis at
**different** stopping potentials ✓ Here they do not, so the comparison is purely one of
intensity, and the graph permits a definite conclusion.
**Why doubling the intensity doubles the current.** Twice as many photons arrive per
second, so twice as many electrons are ejected - each still with the same maximum
energy ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **I₁ = I₂** ✗ would give two coincident curves. **I₁ > I₂**
✗ reverses the reading of the graph. **Comparison is not possible** ✗ ignores the plain
difference in saturation levels ✓
∴ I₁ < I₂.

A pure resistor neither stores nor delays energy, so **voltage and current are in
phase**.
**Step 1 — apply Ohm's law instantaneously.** For a resistor, at every instant,
V = IR ✓
With V = V₀ sin ωt,
I = (V₀/R) sin ωt
**Step 2 — compare the two.** Both are sine functions of **the same argument ωt**, with
no phase offset ✓ They peak together, cross zero together and reverse together, so the
**phase difference is zero**.
**Why a resistor behaves this way.** It has no mechanism for storing energy ✓ An
inductor stores energy in a magnetic field and a capacitor in an electric field, and
that storage is what introduces a delay between voltage and current. A resistor converts
energy to heat immediately, with no lag.
**The contrast with the other elements.**
**resistor**: φ = **0** - in phase ✓
**inductor**: current **lags** voltage by **90°** - "**L**ags" for **L**
**capacitor**: current **leads** voltage by **90°** ✓
The mnemonic **CIVIL** - in a **C**, **I** leads **V**; **V** leads **I** in an **L** -
keeps the two straight.
**The power consequence.** With φ = 0, cos φ = 1 and
P = V_rms I_rms ✓
A resistor consumes power throughout the cycle; a pure inductor or capacitor consumes
**none** on average, since cos 90° = 0.
**The instantaneous power in a resistor.**
P = V₀I₀ sin²ωt
which is **never negative** ✓ Energy always flows from the source into the resistor,
never back - unlike a reactive element, which returns energy each quarter-cycle.
**Reading the distractors.** **Voltage leads by 90°** ✗ describes a pure **inductor**.
**Current leads by 90°** ✗ describes a pure **capacitor**. **Current leads by 180°** ✗
describes no circuit element at all - that would mean the current flows backwards
whenever the voltage is forward, which no passive component does ✓
∴ voltage and current are in same phase with each other.
